Haier split units run on the computed Haier family, which sends the 176-bit, 160-bit and YR-W02 112-bit frames in a single press, so it drives an HSU wall unit whichever YR-series remote it shipped with. 205 Haier code sets are also published. No change needed; unverified against this unit.

Eolia F-series, remote ACXF00-14780. Asked twice (2026-09-14, 2026-09-16, the second from 1.4.1). IR is not a route and will not be: the 21 Panasonic AC packs we hold are all export A75C-family captures, Flipper-IRDB's five Panasonic AC files hold no ACXF00, and IRremoteESP8266 — the reference for this protocol — implements only NKE, DKE, JKE, CKP and RKR, every one identified by an A75C or CS- remote. The Japanese domestic Eolia framing has no public encoder to build a family from.

Comfort Cloud is the only way to drive this unit, and two things had to be true. The Auth0 sign-in rewrite (3e29323) is in v1.5-b2, so that part already shipped. But AddDeviceConfigView.transportOptions never listed .panasonic — nor MELCloud, ThinQ, SmartHQ, De'Longhi, Sensibo, SmartThings, ConnectLife or SwitchBot — so the transport could not be selected at all. Fixed in c9b1ab0, held for the next release. Until that build ships there is nothing this customer can do, and the transport has still never been run against a real account.

AMX100 is a white-label mini Android projector also sold as Sainellor, Amovfilm and AimeiSen; no capture exists for it in Flipper-IRDB or irdb under any of those names. LEC added as an alias of the generic captures, and those six sets now also surface under the name Generic instead of only BrandUnknown. Whether they drive an AMX100 is unverified — learning the remote is the reliable path.

Asked twice on 2026-09-16, both in Japanese. R5.0-D is the remote, not the light: it ships with the LED ceiling lights of the 5.0 series (CL6D-5.0 and siblings), and CL-RL1 is the current replacement part; R5.0-DL / CL-RL2 are the colour-temperature variants.

I reported that no codes existed anywhere. That was wrong — I had checked Flipper-IRDB and irdb and stopped. SmartIR has an Iris Ohyama ceiling light, LEDHCL-R2, now shipped as smartir-1000-iris-ohyama: on, off, power and brightness up/down. It also has NEC (RE0201-CH2) and Takizumi (TLR-002) ceiling lights, which is three more Japanese lights than we had.

Not the same model as the 5.0 series, so unverified for this customer — Japanese ceiling lights from one maker often share a code set across the range, which is the bet worth offering them. Off is two frames sent in sequence, joined with a 40 ms gap; a first pass dropped it entirely by only reading string commands, which is fixed in the importer.

Status stays in_progress until someone confirms it drives an R5.0-D light.

Closed 2026-09-23 by the irext re-import. The earlier reading — that no public source had Iris Ohyama — was doubly wrong: it counted remote_index (10 lights) rather than collect_remote (147), and it treated the collect_* database as unpublished when it is irext/database itself. There are eight Iris Ohyama bulb remotes, now shipped as irext-6899..6906-iris-ohyama, three keys each: power, brightness up and brightness down. An Iris Ohyama row was added to brands.json under light so they are reachable. Also three Iris Ohyama fans came in the same import. Not verified against hardware — these are irext's own captures.

Non-smart 1080p US set (its own quick-start manual lists no Wi-Fi or smart features; remote EN-22655S), so it is IR only — no Roku or network transport applies despite the Roku-era Q naming. Sharp was already in the picker, but the curated pack it leads to, sharp-tv-01, held generic NEC numbers tagged as the Sharp protocol: Power sent OBC 1, the digit "1". Rebuilt from the canonical Sharp map (address 1, plus Sharp's second device 17 for transport and discrete power), 12 buttons to 48, verified bit-for-bit against the Flipper captures we ship. Published as v2 in manifest v28, so installed builds pick it up. Not tested on a Sharp TV. Request arrived in Spanish, no region given.

Already supported — no change needed. "LCDprojector" with "power: AC100-260V" is how these arrive: the customer reads the box, not a model plate. It is the HY300 family, covered by magcubic-hy300-01/-02 (the two remotes these ship with) with Smoon and SU.YOSO aliased to it. Deliberately not adding "LCD projector" as a searchTerm — it would claim every projector in the catalogue. Asked twice in two days (2026-09-16 French/macOS 1.4, 2026-09-17 Portuguese/iOS 1.5), both naming the model "LCD projector" — the box name is what people have. First requester is on macOS 1.4 (build 25G83, French UI), so a Wi-Fi or Bluetooth bridge is the only option: the Mac build drops the USB and audio blasters.

Filed under Custom Remote, which is the tell that the TV brand list came up empty. ROCH is an African appliance label (Ghana/Nigeria/Tanzania) that rebadges Chinese ODM sets; nothing under that name exists in brands.json, our packs, Flipper-IRDB or irdb, and the model is just "Smart tv", so there is no chassis to match on. Deliberately not adding a brand row: with no alias it leads to the synthesized NEC fallback, which will not work, and guessing an alias is worse. Asked for the number printed on the remote — that is what would identify the ODM. Note the brand sweep is weak here: it cycles IRDatabase.brands (the compiled 42 plus cloud rows) blasting synthesized codes, not the 546 brands that have real packs; the Code Database is the tool to point at.

Another HY300-class white label. BOSEN (博森生活, bosenlife.com.tw) is a Taiwanese direct-sale brand; the product profile is the HY300 family — Android mini projector, built-in YouTube/Netflix/Disney+, phone casting, NT$1,680–3,280 — so aliased to Magcubic like Smoon and SU.YOSO before it, and the two HY300 remote sets should drive it. Weaker evidence than the Smoon alias, which had a model match (Smoon 320 = HY 320): "二代升級版" is marketing copy, not a model, so this is inference from the product profile alone and nobody has seen the remote. If it turns out wrong, drop the aliasOf — learning the remote is the fallback either way.

The button list in the request is the XRT122 — Power, V.Link, Vol, Mute, Input, CC, Ch, Picture Mode, Play/Pause — and we ship a capture of exactly that remote (flip-vizio-xrt122), which agrees with the rebuilt vizio-tv-01 on every shared key. Three of the customer's buttons were missing from the curated pack, so added from the capture consensus at NEC 04 FB: Closed Caption 57 (9/9 remotes), Picture Mode 103 (3/3), Play 51 / Pause 55, plus stop, rewind, fast-forward, dash and Disney+. V.Link is the one button with no code in any capture — nothing maps to it. `previous` also decodes to 26, which collides with lastChannel; kept lastChannel.

Veho's own product, not a white label: Quda PJ-1 "ROHM", Android 11, Wi-Fi 6, native 1280x720 scaling 4K, 1.2:1 throw, £179.95. Deliberately NOT aliased to Magcubic — the HY300 class it superficially resembles sells at a quarter the price with different internals, and the BOSEN alias rested on that price/spec profile matching, which this does not. No codes anywhere: no Veho in brands.json, our packs, Flipper-IRDB (Projectors has no Veho/Quda/ROHM folder) or irdb.

It did surface a gap worth fixing: the projector category offered no Wi-Fi scan and no androidTV/chromecast transport, though these projectors run Android. Added in 41d768d as a .projector case rather than by flipping isTypicallyNetwork, which would also have offered Roku, Samsung, LG, Sony and Apple TV. Held for the next release, and unverified — whether a given Android projector advertises the Android TV remote service is unknown. Learning the remote is the path meanwhile.

The remote number is the answer: YAC1FB is a GREE-family part, sold as a replacement for Gree, Trane and Electrolux units. Tadiran had no computed family at all — it is not in GreeAC.brands or any compiled family, and its brands.json row carried no `family`, so ACProtocolRegistry.family(for:) returned nil and the brand fell back to whatever CloudIRService.brandAliases gave it, which is Carrier: twelve irx captures that will not match a GREE remote. Now `family: gree`, which the compiled GreeAC encoder answers, so it needs no build. Also searchable by the remote numbers and by תדיראן.

Scope caveat: this routes every Tadiran AC to gree, and Tadiran (Israel) sources from several Chinese OEMs over the years, so an older unit may not match. Evidence is this customer's remote, not the brand as a whole — but nil was the alternative. Request came in Thai, which fits a grey-import or a regional rebadge rather than the Israeli line.

Gulf house brand rebadging Chinese ODM sets, same shape as req-033 (ROCH, Tanzania): nothing under the name in brands.json, our packs, Flipper-IRDB or irdb, and the model field just repeats the brand, so there is no chassis to match. No brand row added — without an alias it leads to the synthesized NEC fallback, and an alias would be a guess. Asked for the number on the remote. Requester is on macOS 1.4 (build 25G83).

Second one this week, which makes the pattern worth a decision: BrandSweepView is the feature built for exactly this — unknown rebadge, try everything — but it cycles IRDatabase.brands blasting synthesized code sets, so it never reaches the 546 brands that have real packs. Pointing it at the manifest's most common TV code sets instead would make it answer the question it exists to answer.

Under-specified rather than spam — the fields differ, so it does not match the triage pattern, but "Knnb" is not a model and "Mas" matches none of the 255 fan brands we hold. Tried the Arabic-keyboard-layout reading (k→ن, n→ى, b→لا) and it decodes to nothing, so it is most likely a customer who does not know what they have. Asked for the remote's number or a photo. Nothing added.

Worth noting for the fan category specifically: we hold 658 fan packs but only four curated ones (COSMOS wall fan, Dyson, a generic 3-speed ceiling fan, Honeywell), so the rebuilt sweep has very little to work with here compared with TV's 29. The generic 3-speed ceiling fan pack is the one most likely to answer a no-name remote.

The remote number identified a whole family we did not have. YKR-* is the Electra protocol in IRremoteESP8266 (ir_Electra.h), which lists AUX YKR-T/011, Electra YKR-M/003E, Subtropic YKR-H/102E and Centek YKR-P/002E — one digit from this customer's YKR-P/001E — plus Electrolux, AEG, Frigidaire and Delonghi models.

Built as a computed family: 13 bytes, LSB-first, header 9166/4470, bit 646, one 1647, zero 547, byte 0 = 0xC3, temp in byte 1 bits 3-7 (offset 8), swing byte 1 bits 0-2, fan byte 4 bits 5-7, mode byte 6 bits 5-7, power byte 9 bit 5, byteSum(0..11) into byte 12. Verified three ways: the layout against IRremoteESP8266; the checksum and every field byte against our flip-subtropic-in-07hn1 capture (6/6 frames, bytes 0-8 and 10 exact); and the descriptor against an independent Python encoder over the whole state grid through the app's own interpreter (680/680 states byte for byte).

Two knowing divergences from that capture. Byte 11 is the light-toggle byte, which the captured remote varies per press — we send IRremoteESP8266's idle value 0x08. And the remote blanks the temperature field in fan and auto, which the descriptor cannot express (setBytes runs before fields, and fields OR in), so we send it; the unit has no target temperature in those modes.

Routed AMENA, AUX, Electra, Subtropic and Centek to the family. Deliberately not Electrolux, Frigidaire or DeLonghi: IRremoteESP8266 lists one model each, they build many others, and they already have capture packs a wrong family would override.

IRremoteESP8266 has a Voltas protocol (ir_Voltas.{h,cpp}, "122LZF 4011252 Window A/C" — this customer's 4503627 is the same shape of part number). Built it: 10 bytes, 80 bits, no header at all, bit mark 1026, one 2553, zero 554, LSB-first; mode in byte 1 bits 0-3 (fan 1, heat 2, dry 4, cool 8), fan in bits 5-7, power in byte 2 bit 7, temp-16 in byte 3 bits 0-3 with bit 4 always set, 0x33 / 0x3B x3 / 0x11 fixed, ~byteSum(0..8) into byte 9. No auto mode — the library falls back to cool and so do we; dry pins fan low and temp 24.

Needed a new checksum type, byteSumComplement, added to ACProtocolInterpreter — so the descriptor activates on builds after 2026-09-20 and older ones drop it and use voltas-ac-01, which is the documented compatibility path.

Evidence is thinner than Electra's and the docs say so: the reference encoder reproduces IRremoteESP8266's kReset byte for byte (33 28 00 17 3B 3B 3B 11 00 CB) and the descriptor agrees with it on 680/680 states through the app's interpreter, but there was no capture to check against — our two Voltas packs are irext and neither is this protocol, and Flipper-IRDB has no Voltas AC. Built on request with that caveat understood.

Same shape as BOSEN (req-034): a marketplace name on the generic Android mini projector, and the model field is the OS version because there is no model. The product profile is the HY300 class — Android 11, 720p native claiming 1080p/4K support, WiFi 6, 180-degree rotation, 1GB/8GB, $40-70 — so aliased to Magcubic like Smoon, SU.YOSO and BOSEN, and the two HY300 remote sets should drive it.

Inference from the product profile, not a capture; nobody has seen the remote. The contrast is req-036, the Veho Quda, which was NOT aliased: Veho's own line at £180 with Wi-Fi 6 and a 1.2:1 throw does not fit the class however similar it looks. Price band and marketplace-brand pattern are what separate the two.

Solved from a source we were not using. I had checked Flipper-IRDB, irdb and IRremoteESP8266 and reported that nothing public had Unionaire — wrong: SmartIR (smartHomeHub/SmartIR, MIT) has codes/climate/2140.json, manufacturer Unionaire, model Artify, which is this customer's unit. Broadlink base64, decoded at 269/8192 ms per tick into raw durations and shipped as unionaire-ac-01: 73 tokens, off plus cool and heat 20-28C with auto/low/medium/high.

Frames check out as real captures: 64 bits each, cool.24 to cool.25 differs in three bit positions (temperature plus checksum), cool.24 to cool.24.low in four. Nothing reverse-engineered — these are the remote's own signals.

Coverage is what the file has: no auto, dry or fan mode, and 20-28C only. The brand row carries KUSAN, Artify and يونيونير as search terms.

The bigger finding is SmartIR itself: 358 climate device files, 56 media_player, 17 fan, all MIT and all real captures keyed by mode/fan/temperature. Air conditioning is where our coverage is thinnest because state protocols need an encoder, and this is a database of captures that sidesteps that. Worth a proper import.

The naming trap, exactly as the runbook has it: SRK is Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, not Mitsubishi Electric. The customer chose Mitsubishi, where nothing will drive their unit. Already supported under Mitsubishi Heavy — mitsubishi-ac-02 covers all SRK/SRC on the compiled family (145 buttons), and today's SmartIR import added SRK25ZJ-S1/SRK13CRV-S1 and SRK71ZK-S at 157 each. Searching SRK already reaches it; the brand row has carried that term for a while. Nothing to add for the request itself.

It did expose a mess the SmartIR import made: the brand-row generator created 'Mitsubishi Heavy Industries', 'Mitsubishi Electric Starmex' and 'Ggeneral Electric' (SmartIR's own typo) as separate brands from ones we already had, each with one pack and no family. Aliased to their canonical rows so picking either shows both sets. A name-overlap scan of the whole table found no others worth merging: Eberg/Leberg, Royal Clima/ROYAL, Subtropic/Tropic and Westinghouse/White-Westinghouse are all genuinely different marques.

Sylvox is an outdoor-TV brand (deck, pool, bathroom sets) and OT43A0KAGB is the 43" Deck Series, 2023. It runs Android TV 11 with Chromecast built in, which is the whole answer: TV is isTypicallyNetwork, so Add Device -> TV already offers Scan Wi-Fi for Devices plus Android TV (Pair with PIN) and Chromecast. Full control on 1.5 today, no IR bridge and no update. openhoangnc/android_model_name carries SYLVOX Google TV / 4K Google TV-A..E, confirming the platform.

No IR codes shipped, deliberately. Sylvox is absent from Flipper-IRDB, irdb and SmartIR (GitHub code search, all three, control query proves the search works); the only 'sylv' packs we hold are flip-sylvania-* and irext-*-sylvania, a different marque entirely - do not alias them. The Deck Series remote is IR (replacement remotes advertise 'no programming, 2x AAA'), so codes exist to be captured, we just have none.

A bare brand row would have been worse than nothing: IRDatabase.signal falls back to synthesized(for:) for a cloud brand with no packs, so Sylvox would appear in the picker backed by invented addresses and look supported while working only by coincidence. Same trap as the sweep before 275e3fc. Revisit if a capture turns up.

"It says it failed", with no more than that: the mail came through the review gate, so this customer has 10+ successful commands behind them, and 1.5 predates the support-mail diagnostics (771e1e8, unreleased), so there is nothing else in it.

Ruled out delivery. verify_published.py b315ec25 (the commit is the rev, not a range - b315ec25..HEAD excludes the packs it added) reads both magcubic-hy300-01 and -02 clean against the live manifest HMAC on all five providers. Not an integrity failure.

Ruled out malformed codes. Decrypted both: plain NEC with device/subdevice/function, no raw timings, so any bridge can encode them. -01 is NEC 00/FF, 12 keys, power function 0x14; -02 is NEC 01/FE, 13 keys, power 0x40. Better, 0x14 is corroborated by the projector's own factory firmware - shift/sun50iw12p1-research reverse-engineered the H713 DTB and its cir_param node carries ir_power_key_code0 = <0x14>. That is the first outside confirmation these codes have ever had; b315ec25 never claimed a source.

Most likely the remote variant. The HY300 shipped two remotes on different NEC addresses, which is why there are two packs, and the factory property is indexed (code0) as if the firmware expects more than one. If they picked remote 1, remote 2 is the next thing to try. Second candidate is a send-time transport failure: the red cross and message come from AddDeviceConfigView's Test, which reports the last log entry's detail, not anything about the code set.

Nothing changed. Waiting on which code set they picked and the exact wording.

An empty mail: no words at all, just the diagnostics footer and "Được gửi từ iPhone của tôi". Vietnamese, 1.5 (2), iOS 18.6. Nothing to diagnose and nobody to ask without a reply.

The cause is ours. ReviewPrompter.feedbackURL built the body as "\n\n\n---\nApp: ...", so tapping Send Feedback opened a blank mail above a technical footer with nothing saying what to write. A customer who does not read English gets no cue at all. This is the second near-empty one - an earlier Vietnamese report was the three characters "Mo ko dc" (Vietnamese shorthand for "mở không được", can't get it to open/turn on) - and both came through the review gate, which only offers the mail after a 10/50/100 success milestone. These are customers with working setups and something specific to say.

Fixed in 787911d: a localized prompt line above the blank lines, in all 35 languages, verified by reading the compiled Localizable.strings back out of the built app. Compiled text, not a cloud id, so it reaches anyone only in the next release. The subject stays English so the inbox still sorts.

Reply sent in Vietnamese asking what the device is and what happens.

Third instance, 2026-09-21, Indonesian: "jelek aneh apk nya" — bad, weird, that is the whole report. Same shape as the other two: 1.5 (2), through the review gate so 10+ successful commands, and no cue in the mail about what to write. Also the first that is a complaint about the app rather than a device failing, which the prompt line in 787911d should separate out — someone with a working setup who dislikes something has no other way to say what. Still unreleased, so the next few of these will look the same.

Fourth instance, 2026-09-28, Russian: "Не понятно ничего" - "none of it makes sense". 1.5 (2), iOS 26.3.1, through the review gate, so ten or more successful commands. Like the Indonesian one, a complaint about the app rather than a device failing: something works for this customer and the rest is opaque. Possibly the Yoshoot Y05 customer of req-061 (Russian, iOS 26.3.1), whose request got no codes - not established; the footer carries no identity. Reply drafted in Russian: what are you trying to control, a one-paragraph model of the app (Wi-Fi devices direct, IR devices through a bridge), and the in-app guide at Settings > Help & Buy Hardware > Getting Started.

Fifth and sixth instances, 2026-09-30, both English, 1.5 (2), iOS 26.6.1, "Sent from my iPhone": one reading only "Worst app", and one from Trilok Gole with no body at all - the mail client's header text and the footer, nothing typed. Same version, OS and sign-off on the same day, so possibly one customer writing twice; not established. Nothing to act on in either. Replies ask what they are trying to control and give the same short model of the app as the Russian one; the "Worst app" reply also states the free tier (one device, no ads), since that complaint is usually the paywall.

"Luminous led", model E501, region "Nhật" - Vietnamese for Japan, and the customer writes Vietnamese. Luminous is Doshisha's LED ceiling-light line and E501 is the remote, not the light: it ships with the E50-U06D/U08D/U12D and E50-V06D/V08D/V12D fixtures (kaname78's parts catalogue lists the set, JAN 4550283308707).

Nothing public had the codes - absent from SmartIR, Flipper-IRDB and irdb - but IRremoteESP8266 has a whole Doshisha protocol in ir_Doshisha.cpp, which none of those searches would have surfaced: AEHA-shaped, header 3412/1722, bit mark 420, spaces 1310/452, 38kHz, 40 bits MSB-first, framed as 0x800B3048 plus a command byte masked 0xFE and a channel bit. It names the commands too: On 0xC0, Off 0xA0, level up 0xCC, level down 0x2C, night light 0xC8, four discrete levels.

Encoder checked against the three real captures in test/ir_Doshisha_test.cpp and it reproduces 800B3048A5, 800B3048A1 and 800B3048A0 exactly; the sealed packs decode back to the same frames. Shipped as doshisha-light-01/02, one per channel like the Magcubic remotes, four keys each - the protocol has discrete On and Off and no toggle, so no fifth key was invented. Manifest v44, clean on all five providers.

The gap worth remembering: upstream's "works on real device" covers the RCZ01 remote and the CZ-S32D/S38D/S50D lights. This customer has the later E501 and an E50-* fixture. Same maker, same product line, protocol assumed to carry over and not verified against their hardware. If they come back saying it does nothing, that assumption is the thing that broke, and the next step is asking them to learn a button rather than guessing again.

"Celasin" resolves to nothing — not in brands.json, our 672 fan packs, Flipper-IRDB or irdb, and no product under that name turns up publicly; most likely a Shopee or Lazada marketplace name, or a misspelling. The model field is the product description in Vietnamese (an evaporative air cooler / circulator), and the region field says "Phòng khách" — living room — so the form was filled loosely and there is no identifier in it at all.

No brand row: nothing to alias it to, and with no family it would lead to the synthesized NEC fallback. Asked for the number on the remote or a photo. Learning is a better answer than usual here — a fan remote is five or six buttons, so copying it through a bridge takes a minute, unlike an AC where every temperature is its own frame.

Arabic mail signature, and EPS30(PS) is a 16-inch Toshiba wall fan sold all over Egypt (2B, B.TECH, Raya, EHAB): 3 speeds, oscillation, 8-hour timer, 220V 65W. So the button set is power, speed, swing, timer.

The find was that we already had a plausible pack and no way to reach it. flip-toshiba-fwsa20 is a real Toshiba fan capture - NEC device 0x4B, subdevice 0x14, functions power 0x80, speed 0x20, oscillate 0xC0, timer 0xA0 - exactly the four an EPS30 needs. But IRDatabase's compiled fan catalogue is only Universal, Honeywell and Dyson, and the Toshiba cloud row listed tv, airConditioner and mediaPlayer, so Toshiba never appeared in the fan brand picker. The pack was reachable through the Code Database and nowhere else. Adding "fan" to the row fixes it with no release.

Also added توشيبا to the search terms - the Arabic spelling matched nothing at all before, which matters for a brand whose mail arrives in Arabic - plus EPS and FWSA so a fan model number lands on the brand the way RAS and CT- already do.

No EPS30 codes claimed. Flipper-IRDB, irdb and SmartIR have nothing for EPS30, Toshiba fan or El Araby. Worth writing down as a naming trap: Toshiba-branded fans and small appliances in Egypt are built by Toshiba El Araby, the joint venture with El Araby Group, not by Toshiba Japan - so the RAS/CT-/REGZA families say nothing about them, and FWSA20 matching is a hope rather than a finding. Checked the sibling theory too: El Araby's own Tornado brand appears only as air conditioners in our packs, no fans to compare against, and cosmos-fan-01 (COSMOS 16-WFGR, the other Egyptian wall fan we hold) is raw with 1200/400 marks and no NEC leader, so it is a different remote family entirely.

Told the customer to try the Toshiba fan set and to say if it does nothing; learning their own remote is the fallback, and that needs a Broadlink or Tuya hub - the only two transports that implement learn.

Portuguese, Barcarena-PA. Two things in one mail, and the note is the real request: "Conectar no Fire tv Stick na minha tv sem conexao a o Wi-Fi" - they want to drive a Fire TV Stick with no Wi-Fi.

That cannot be done, and the reason is hardware. A Fire TV Stick has no IR receiver at all; its bundled remote is Bluetooth. IR universal remotes do not control a Stick, and the only workaround is an external USB IR receiver (Inteset IReTV) in its micro-USB port. Without Wi-Fi our Android TV and ADB paths are out too, so there is no route left.

Which exposes a pack we should not be shipping: firetv-stb-01, "Amazon / Fire TV Stick", streamingBox, 18 buttons. It promises exactly what the hardware cannot do. English ("Sent from my iPhone"), App 1.5, iOS 26.6.2. No notes and no region, so the model is the whole request. The DVP-SR200P is a compact Sony DVD player that ships with the RMT-D197A remote. Sony DVD players speak 20-bit SIRC: device 26, extended 73. Flipper writes a SIRC20 address as 13 bits across two bytes (3A 09 = 0x093A), and import_flipper.py kept only the first byte and filed every SIRC variant as 12-bit "sony". So every button went out as device 26 on a 12-bit frame, which no DVD player answers. Every Sony Blu-ray pack had the same fault (26/226, stored as 5A 1C), and so did the SIRC15 codes on Sony TVs, projectors and soundbars: 712 codes wrong across 50 packs.

Fixed in the cloud, so installed builds get it. We regenerated 61 Flipper packs: those 50, plus 11 whose SIRC12 codes had the right address but went out once. Each code is now three frames at a 45 ms period and 40 kHz. Sony receivers expect at least three frames; Flipper, IRremoteESP8266 and LIRC all send three, and every shipped build of ours sends one. The curated sony-bd-01 turned out to be invented (TV cursor codes on a 12-bit frame), so it was rebuilt from the 14 Sony Blu-ray captures. sony-tv-01..03 kept their codes and became three-frame bursts.

Checked by decoding: the DVD pack's keys match irdb's Sony DVD 26/73 functions one for one (power 21, open/close 22, menu 27, cursor 121-124, enter 11, return 14, play 50, pause 57, stop 56). Not verified on hardware.

Also added sony-dvd-01, "DVP-SR / DVP-NS Series". No brand had a curated DVD pack, so Find My Remote Automatically could never have found a DVD player. Its 29 keys are the ones both Sony DVD captures share, each named the same in irdb 26/73, and byte-identical to the RMT-D197A pack.

What to tell them: Browse Full Code Database, then Sony, then "DVD RMT-D197A". Choosing only the brand saves placeholder NEC codes. A player added earlier keeps the codes it was saved with, so pick the code set again from the remote's Code Database menu.

Hisense is in 1.5's compiled AC list but has no family, compiled or in brands.json. So a Hisense AC added by brand sends the synthesized NEC set (address 0C; power is 0C F3 02 FD), which no air conditioner answers. All 27 Hisense AC packs are sealed, and so are the 11 Kelon ones. On 1.5 each one fails the integrity check, although the code browser lists them under Our Cloud.

Two Brazilian replacement-remote listings (Mix Eletro, Dupatu) name the AS-12TW2RLDTT00 among the units the DG11L1-03 fits. Hisense's DG11-series split remotes share one frame. It is 21 bytes starting 83 06, sent in sections of 6, 8 and 7 bytes, with a 9000/4500 header and about 8 ms between sections. Byte 13 holds the XOR of bytes 2-12 and byte 20 the XOR of bytes 14-19. The temperature minus 16 is in the high nibble of byte 3, the mode is in its low bits, and the fan is in byte 2. IRremoteESP8266 decodes this frame as KELON168 (DG11R2-01) and also as WHIRLPOOL, model DG11J191. An open ESPHome PR (hisense_arg, esphome#17352) reverse-engineered the same frame from the Hisense codec in BGH's Smart Control, an IR controller sold in Argentina. Every Hisense or Kelon split capture we hold that names a remote or model decodes to it: Flipper's DG11J1-99, AS-30HR4SQBTD and Kelon AS-24HR4SQJUL, and SmartIR's DG11R2-01 (smartir-1522) and AS-07UR4SYDD815G (smartir-5520). So does the one public capture from a DG11L1 remote, a DG11L1-12 power press posted in ToniA/arduino-heatpumpir#126 (2021): 83 06 04 71 00 00 80 02 00 00 00 00 00 F7 00 01 00 00 08 00 09, at 8911/4547 with 8 ms gaps, both checksums correct. There is no DG11L1-03 capture, so this remote's format is inferred from that sibling, not seen.

Power in this format is a toggle: bit 2 of byte 2, with command byte 15 = 01. Other frames carry the button pressed in byte 15 (02 temperature, 06 mode, 11 fan), and by IRremoteESP8266 and the ESPHome code they do not switch a unit on. Byte 18 varies. It is 08 in the Argentine codec, in DG11J1-99, in the DG11L1-12 capture and in smartir-5520, and 28 (off) or 38 (on) in DG11R2-01.

This is not a family, for two reasons. The compiled whirlpool family sends this frame for the DG11J1-3A model (temperature minus 18, byte 18 = 00). It also sets the toggle bit in every frame while the unit is on. Routed there, a Hisense would read every setpoint 2 degrees low, and a unit that honours the bit would toggle power at each press. And on 1.5 a Hisense descriptor cannot send the toggle at the right moment, because its button variable calls a mode press "power".

So smartir-5520-hisense and smartir-1522-hisense go into REQUESTED and publish plaintext. Both are full grids of 241 frames: off, plus cool, heat, dry and fan at 16-30 with four fan settings. Every frame passes both checksums. smartir-5520 comes first: its byte 18 is the DG11L1-12's 08, and its only toggle frame is off. Three of smartir-1522's frames (cool.16, heat.30 and fan.16, all fan auto) are power-button captures that would switch the unit. Neither pack has auto-mode frames. The irext packs of the same shape (irx-11241, irx-3474, irx-3475 and irx-11257-kelon) leave byte 13 at zero in all 27 frames, so they stay sealed.

The reply sends the customer to Browse Full Code Database > Our Cloud > Hisense, AS-07UR4SYDD815G first and then DGR11R2, through an IR blaster, since 1.5 offers no ConnectLife route. On 1.5 Test Power sends the off frame, which here is the power toggle, so it should switch the unit either way. 1.5's own Power key sends a settings frame when switching on. So the reply says to tap Power until the unit starts and then pick a mode, which brings the app back in step. It also says how to pull a fresh manifest if a set still errors, and asks for the code on the remote if neither set works. Decoded, not tested on a Hisense unit.

Worth building later: a Hisense family from this frame, once a release lets a descriptor see a power transition. It would cover Hisense and Kelon splits without a pack.

Two mails, one customer (the maintainer tied them together). English sign-off (Sent from my iPhone), so one English reply. App 1.5, iOS 26.4 (23E246). The first typed Haier into every field and lost its first letter ("ategory") in pasting. The second typed AA8ZD7E0300INHCCA250 into Model, Region and Notes. Identical fields are not the spam pattern here: the second mail carries a real Haier barcode.

The barcode is Haier's 20-character serial: a 13-character product code, three date characters and a 4-character sequence. Haier India's and Haier Pakistan's serial pages describe it, and a Haier Russia AC manual gives the same date positions. HCC is the date: H = 2017, C = December, C = 12th, so the unit was built on 12 December 2017. Haier codes never contain I or O ("I is a 1", Haier India), so the IN is 1N. No source documents a market code anywhere in the string, so it does not say India. The product code AA8ZD7E03 is in no public listing, so the model, the market and the remote are all unknown.

What 1.5 does, read from v1.5-b2: Haier is 12th in the compiled AC list, after Hitachi. Picking it gives codeSetID airConditioner.haier, and the compiled map routes it to the haier family ahead of brands.json. HaierAC.signal then sends the 176-bit (A6 ... B7), 160-bit (A6 ... B5) and 112-bit YR-W02 frames back to back, 40 ms apart, at 3000/3000 + 3000/4300 and 520/1650/650, MSB first. That is 913 durations, about 0.72 s. It covers YR-W02, V9014557 (IRremoteESP8266's HAIER_AC176, and model A of its YRW02) and the 160-bit KFR-26GW units. The encoder has not changed since 76dbc50, which v1.5-b2 contains. Nothing in the cloud can change it: the compiled family outranks brands.json, and the compiled encoder outranks protocols.json.

Of 44 Haier AC packs, only two are plaintext: haier-ac-01 (155 frames, the 176-bit frame alone) and haier-ac-02 (152 frames, the same three-frame burst). Both match the compiled encoder duration for duration, so importing either changes nothing. The other 42 are sealed and fail on 1.5. Our Cloud > Haier shows 52 rows on 1.5, because robot-vacuum and purifier packs match the ac and air keywords. haier-ac-02 is 4th and haier-ac-01 is 44th.

The gap is Haier's 72-bit frame. It is 9 bytes, starting A5, with the temperature in the high nibble of byte 1 and a command in the low nibble, the sum of bytes 0-7 as checksum, and the same timings. IRremoteESP8266 decodes it as HAIER_AC, from an HSU07-HEA03 remote. Both YR-H10 dumps in IRremoteESP8266 #435 decode to it (power off: A5 80 34 1C 0C 80 20 00 21). So do SmartIR #888's YR-D01 codes for an HSU-12HA03 split (A5 00 21 1A 0C 80 20 00 8C). A HarmonyOS encoder (devvanglin/harmonyos-smart-home) says its 9-byte timings were measured on a YR-M10, and YR-M10-compatible replacements are sold in India. 1.5 sends this frame for no brand. Seven irext packs carry it (irx-3523, -3530, -3531, -3543, -3544, -3545 and -3555), but they are sealed, and their on-state frames carry the temp-up or fan command rather than On. In #435 the library's author thought it "quite possible" that a temp-up frame did not switch the unit on. The compiled HaierAC9 is never called, and it maps fan low and high the wrong way round (IRremoteESP8266 sends 3 for low and 1 for high).

The fix is haier-ac-03, a curated pack. Its model, "Alternative 72-bit remotes: YR-D01 / YR-H10 / YR-M10 / HSU07-HEA03", lists 5th on 1.5, right after haier-ac-02. It holds 152 frames on haier-ac-02's grid. Every on-state frame carries command On and the off frame carries Off, as IRac::haier sends them. Byte 2 bit 5 is set, as in every capture, and the fan uses IRremoteESP8266's values. Each frame is 149 durations, about 110 ms. The reference encoder reproduces #404's real capture byte for byte (A5 01 20 01 00 C0 20 00 A7, with its clock minute). The pack is plaintext by its id, so it opens on 1.5. No brands.json or protocols.json change.

The reply starts with the brand route. On 1.5 an air conditioner opens on Midea Smart AC (Wi-Fi), and Brand only appears once an infrared option is chosen, so it says to set Control via first and then pick Haier. It says to ignore Test Connection's "No IR code set is assigned to this device.": the button sends .power, which no AC code set has, on 1.5 and on main. Then it offers the new set, through Browse Full Code Database > Our Cloud > Haier, with the unit switched on first, since Test Power sends the off frame. If the set does not show, Settings > Cloud IR Database, pulled down. It asks for the indoor unit's model and the code on the remote. hOn is not offered. 1.5 does list Haier hOn (Candy, Hoover), but it is Haier Europe's cloud and has never run against a real account, and Haier's AC app in India and Pakistan is HaiSmart.

Unverified: the unit's model, market and remote. haier-ac-03 has not been tried on any Haier unit, and YR-M10's protocol comes from secondary sources only.

Worth building later: the 72-bit frame added to HaierAC's burst, with HaierAC9's fan mapping fixed, so that picking Haier covers these remotes without the code browser. That is app-side and waits for a release.

2026-10-01: built, in the app repo's 0ccd6ce. From the next release picking Haier sends the 72-bit frame too, fourth in its burst, with HaierAC9's fan mapping fixed; its frames are haier-ac-03's, code for code. 1.5 through 1.5.2 still send three frames, so until customers run the release haier-ac-03 remains the way to reach these remotes. Not tested on a Haier unit.

Russian ("Отправлено с iPhone"), App 1.5, iOS 27.0.1. "Moctex" is МосТех typed in Latin lookalikes (the notes say "мостех"): MosTech, Moscow's city platform, whose interactive panels with a built-in PC are in Moscow schools. The customer pasted their own capture, 43 lines of NEC hex from another tool (exported 2025-02-14), labelled by what the panel did - "show desktop", "create folder", "search bar" - which is the panel's PC answering.

Read as the IRremote/Arduino 32-bit convention, bit-reversed per byte: address 0x20, and the digits come out 0x10, 0x11, 0x13...0x1B, sequential, where the bytes as written (08 88 C8 28...) are not. Confirmed against our own data: six TV packs at NEC 0x20 (Flipper RCA, Furrion, Crown, Erisson, Elements, Sankey) send the same codes, digits 3/3 each - a common TV-board code set.

Those packs also named what the customer's labels could not, and corrected two. Power is 0x52 (6/6; the customer saw it as "shutdown with a 5/10 s choice", the panel's power-off countdown), not 0x1C, their "on/off". 0x4B and 0x49 are right and left (6/6), not "select up". 0x0A is Exit (5/6), 0x06 Menu (4/6). Where the references are weak the customer's observation wins: volume on 0x03/0x41 (channel on the TV boards), settings 0x07, back 0x48. Left out: 0x1C, 0x0B, 0x0D, 0x1D, 0x26, 0x59 and the lock key 0x5C, which nobody can name with confidence; and digit 1, never captured.

mostech-panel-01, 20 keys, every one re-encoding to the customer's own hex. Rows MosTech, Moctex and МосТех, the last two aliased, so it is found whichever way it is spelt. Not tested on a panel.
